# Scope and Problem Statement
N-RICH aims to create a national research infrastructure bringing together digital (both digitised and born-digital) cultural heritage materials of all kinds from a wide variety of collection holders. Some will have the in-house infrastructure to make their materials available directly while others will require varying levels of service provision in order to participate meaningfully. This can be distilled down to several key objectives:

- Digital collections should be machine actionable and compute-ready

- Standards and guidelines should be widely adoptable by the majority of collection holders

- Recommendations should target both researcher and public access use cases

- [FAIR](https://www.go-fair.org/) is a reasonable encapsulation of researchers’ broad requirements with respect to data, namely:

  - **Findable** – metadata should be sufficient to allow the construction of a discovery service what will allow a researcher to find the object that they require, and provide enough detail about the identity of the object to verify that its authenticity and suitability.

  - **Accessible** – data and metadata should be available for both human and machine consumption without undue technical or policy barriers. The route to more detailed information (e.g. collection specific metadata) should be clearly signposted.

  - **Interoperable** – as much as possible, common ontologies, terminologies and authorities should be used between collections. Mechanisms for access and retrieval should be standardised for any particular type of material or data.

  - **Reusable** – data and metadata should be preserved for long term access, and provide Persistent Identifiers (PIDs) to ensure ongoing citability. As metadata can be updated over time, versioning should also be supported to ensure referential integrity over the longer term.          

Bearing this in mind, it is not feasible for a cost-effective and scalable infrastructure to meet all possible use cases. Therefore, the aim is to satisfy the majority of common research and public engagement requirements and to provide a “deep-dive" mechanism to reach collection specific data for exceptions. 

The approach taken to designing these recommendations is described in the following “Design principles” sections. These draw from several sources:

- The author’s direct experiences with the design of community-based standards such as IIIF, OCFL, EPUB/A and SWORD (and involvement with others, such as BIBFRAME)

- The author’s work on [EU COST IS1310 Reassembling the Republic of Letters](https://www.republicofletters.net/) envisaging a transnational digital infrastructure for reassembling scattered epistolary materials to support scholarly work and public dissemination, published in [Reassembling the Republic of Letters in the Digital Age](https://univerlag.uni-goettingen.de/handle/3/isbn-978-3-86395-403-1). 

- The [development and evolution of Europeana](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/ten-years-europeana-bringing-europes-cultural-heritage-digital-age) and the associated APIs and Data Model

- Guidelines highlighted in the Review of Standards and Guidelines document, particularly the [IFLA Guidelines for Setting up a Digital Unification Project](https://www.ifla.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/assets/hq/topics/cultural-heritage/documents/digital_unification_guidelines.pdf)

- The various outcomes of the [EU Impulse](https://euimpulse.eu/documents/) project on creating a multi-user virtual environment for cultural heritage. In particular, [Deliverable D3.4: Guidelines on simplification of metadata based on open standards](https://zenodo.org/records/18301994) which explores what is necessary for interoperability with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Re-usable) goals in mind

- Discussions at the N-RICH Partners Away Day, 30 June 2026 (especially with representatives of the National Gallery and Science Museum). 

These recommendations are aimed primarily at materials that can be digitised by 2D scanning or imaging, such as manuscripts, maps, prints, drawings etc. Alongside the standards and guidelines themselves, the aim is to demonstrate a process which can be used to expand the recommendations to a broader range of cultural heritage materials. The primary source materials for this document can be found in the Review of Standards and Guidelines document.
# Design Principles
Most of the principles outlined here are not specific to the cultural heritage domain, since they are derived primarily from simple cost-benefit considerations for any organisation looking to adopting standards. 
## Standards
- Standards should not be costly to implement:

  - Standards should be focussed on addressing a specific problem or requirement. The business case for adopting such a standard can thus be relatively simply constructed.

  - Expansive standards that attempt to solve multiple problems at once tend to be less effective at meeting any of their requirements, more expensive to implement and harder to justify unless an organisation has exactly the same requirements that the standard was designed for.  

  - Good standards should generally be accompanied by a complete reference implementation to prove that the standard is implementable, and to act as a second source of truth in the event of ambiguity.

  - Good standards should also be accompanied by a validation process to enable implementers to verify compliance. If this cannot be easily accomplished then the standard is likely to be insufficiently well specified. 

- Standards should not be costly to maintain:

  - Standards concerning the long-term retention of materials should evolve slowly and thoughtfully with consideration given to backwards compatibility so that material does not have to be frequently reworked to maintain compliance.

  - At the same time, standards do need to accommodate developments in the wider world, especially with respect to software and hardware tools. Otherwise, standards can become an obsolescence and/or security risk in their own right.

  - When standards do evolve in a manner that breaks backwards compatibility, a migration route should be designed (and implemented, to prove it works).

  - Standards need to accompanied by ongoing support, documentation and training to ensure the necessary workplace skills continue to exist.  

- Standards should deliver both short- and long-term benefits

  - A good driver for standards adoption is the availability of tools based on the standards that deliver value to the organisation. This is a more likely outcome if the standard is easy to implement. For example, the rapid adoption of IIIF is partly attributable to the availability of both complete software implementations and “shim” code that enabled existing platforms to be compliant.  

  - Workforce familiarity as a result of effective training and documentation can help to drive standards adoption, but is equally an organisational benefit if it ensures that a longer term workforce skills base is developed so that maintenance and staffing is less of an issue. 

  - Interoperability is a longer term benefit, and therefore less satisfactory as a primary driver for adoption although it can be valuable when considering exit strategies and risk managements.
## Guidelines  
- Guidelines can be more dynamic than standards since they are, by definition, less prescriptive. As such, they can be used by organisations as a strategic tool, to track the changing technology and standards landscape and make appropriate plans within the constraints of organisational resources and timescales   

  - Guidelines can recommend standards and may recommend more than one standard if there is not a single optimal path. In that case, guidelines should discuss the pros and cons of the various approaches, and also indicate possible migration routes or mapping between them. If such routes don’t exist then it is likely the different standards address distinct problem domains.    

  - Guidelines can recommend *how* to implement standards. There are many rather less well-defined or expansive standards that are not cost-effective to implement in their entirety. Guidelines can help identify useful subsets or specific interpretations of such standards which can be more practical and useful, essentially mitigating the problem. This can be particularly valuable when considering interoperability, where focussing overly on handling specific, niche details can hamper progress and limit benefits realisation. Guidelines can sometimes also recommend or discourage the use of certain *versions* of a particular standard for similar reasons. For example, BIBFRAME V2.X is very different and a great improvement on V1.0 which should be avoided since it replicated many of the issues of its predecessor, MARC.  

  - As guidelines operate at a more strategic level than standards they can indicate when standards are becoming obsolete-as happens to all technologies. In this case, they should also identify exit strategies and migration paths. 

Common design pitfalls in standards and guidelines development

- Over prescriptive guidelines or standards can be a significant long term dis-benefit by hampering the use of new technologies and techniques. Good approaches are:

  - Standards should be simple and focussed on a well-defined requirement/problem (see previous).

  - Prescribe only the minimum elements required to achieve the goals of the standard. This reduces both the cost of implementation but also minimises the cost of interoperability and migration efforts downstream. 

  - Evaluate design decisions in terms of what functionalities they prevent as well as what they enable. All standards involve some trade-offs and this is especially true for long term preservation applications. For example, the choice of PDF format for archiving publications was good for human readability but did not consider machine readability as a requirement, not only making subsequent text mining and analytics of such materials difficult but also reducing the effectiveness of accessibility tools such as screen readers. 

  - Beyond the minimal core requirements it may be useful to provide or document an optional extension mechanism that makes a clear distinction between core functionality and functionality that is considered more friable in the long term.    

- Over complex standards that are expensive and time consuming to implement are likely to be avoided on a simple cost basis. Even when there is adoption, it is likely that only a subset of the standard or guideline is implemented (to solve the adoptees particular use case), resulting in multiple incompatible variants that effectively undermine the notion of a standard. As noted above, guidelines can address this issue. 

- Vaguely defined standards suffer from a similar problem, stemming from different interpretations of the standard. Requiring a validation mechanism goes a long way to eliminating such cases.

- Guidelines that recommend inappropriate standards for particular applications can also cause problems. Technologies are not objective creations and should be approached critically. It is important to understand the original design goals for a standard, and also the socio-cultural biases and assumptions under which it was created. A lot of standards in the technology area are very Anglo-centric – making assumptions about names, places and dates that don’t translate well to other cultures. Just because a standard *can* support a particular use case does not mean it is necessarily a *good* solution for that use case.

- Standards often suffer from scope creep over time. Standards gradually expand functionality and use cases through successive versions, each iteration becoming slightly less effective at addressing the original design goals, and generally addressing the newly added goals far less effectively than a dedicated standard. Guidelines can identify these cases and discourage the use of the offending versions or recommend the adoption of a more considered subset.         
## Ensuring standards and guidelines are practical and implementable across institutions with varying capacities
To some extent this question is mainly answered by adopting the best practices and avoiding the pitfalls described above, but with a couple of additional points.

- Guidelines should include case studies that clearly demonstrate the value of adoption to all sizes of organisation, effectively providing business cases for potential adoptees. The construction of these studies can also be a valuable point of engagement with the target community.

- Aim for small, focussed, granular standards that are cheap to implement. A smaller organisation can adopt these more easily over time, since they can validate compliance at each stage and gain a sense of achievement, rather than attempting a large implementation and compliance exercise that is time and resource consuming with a high chance of failure.

- Standards and guideless should change slowly over time, and should be recognised as doing so. This encourages smaller organisations to seek compliance since it is an achievable goal rather than a continuously receding target.  

- Aim for open standards that have open-source implementations so the cost of entry can be close to zero. Larger organisations can help support the development of such tools (and associated training and support) to enable them to be freely available to smaller organisations. IIIF, for example has both commercial and open-source implementations and is supported by a consortium funded by larger libraries and other organisations around the world.
## Ensuring national standards and guidelines remain relevant and adaptable over time
- Guidelines should be recognised as being driven by the community that the guidelines are aimed at rather than imposed externally. This not only provides engagement that helps adoption but also provides a mechanism for developing and maintaining skills and expertise at a national level.

- Ideally, national guidelines should, as much as possible, make use of internationally recognised standards since they will be better supported in the longer term both in terms of technology and skills. Engagement with the international organisations concerned would be a great development opportunity for local staff.

- Avoid defining new standards if possible since, at least to begin with, they are likely to only have local support. Instead, aim to engage with and co-opt existing standards initiatives to guide international standards in the desired direction.

- Define a process and timetable for reviewing and updating the guidelines and engage with local staff to participate – possibly with funding or other support. While the initial work may involve external consultancy, over time this should ideally be reduced to encourage local talent development.
# Recommendations
This section is formatted as a standalone specification document in alignment with W3C documentation approaches. 
## Introduction
These standards and guidelines are the outcome of the N-RICH Digitisation Capabilities Pilot and target cultural heritage digitisation resulting in 2D image artefacts and the associated metadata. Taking inspiration from the IMPULSE Consortium’s  [Deliverable D3.4: Guidelines on simplification of metadata based on open standards](https://zenodo.org/records/18301994) the objective is to stablish a “minimum viable set” of standards and guidelines which should allow the construction of a federated research infrastructure.
### Audience
This document is intended primarily for collection holders digitising material for inclusion in N-RICH. However, it is also of informative for those implementing N-RICH infrastructure and tools.

Terminology

The key words *MUST*, *MUST NOT*, *REQUIRED*, *SHOULD*, *SHOULD NOT*, *RECOMMENDED*, and *OPTIONAL* in this document are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2119).
### Overview   
These recommendations will follow the conceptual workflow used in the Review of Standards and Guidelines.  This is deliberately not an expansive specification and the expectation is that this will extend over time as skills and technology evolve. 

![](data:image/png;base64,)

The specification identifies 3 levels of compliance:

Level 0: Elements identified by key words *MUST, MUST NOT* and *REQUIRED.*

Level 1: Level 0 elements plus those identified by the key words *SHOULD*, *SHOULD NOT* and *RECOMMENDED.*

Level 2: Level 1 elements plus those identified by the key word *OPTIONAL.*

Selection Documentation

Transparency around how and why selections decisions have been made is essential so that the researchers and the public can understand gap between what is available and what exists (or exist*ed*). This information is made available in the documents outlined in the table below. When a document exists, it MUST be made available online, and, for collection or item level documentation, MUST be linked in the metadata for the objects to which they apply.   

| Document  | Requirements |
| --- | --- |
| Collection/Accession Policy – why and how collections and/or items are acquired | MUST be published at organisation levelSHOULD be published at a collection levelOPTIONAL at item level (for special acquisitions) |
| Digitisation Policy – why and how material is selected for digitisation | SHOULD be published at organisation levelSHOULD be published at a collection/project levelOPTIONAL at item level (for special acquisitions) |
| Appraisal/Evaluation Document - why is an item/collection considered culturally significant, at risk and/or unique | OPTIONAL at a collection levelOPTIONAL at item level (for special acquisitions) |
### Recommended reading
The [UNESCO Recommendation Concerning the Preservation of, and Access to, Documentary Heritage Incl. Digital Form (2015)](https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000244675.page=5) goes into considerable detail on good practice for selection processes and the accompanying documentation. 
## Metadata
This section focuses on object metadata that is made available to researchers and the public through the N-RICH shared infrastructure. Metadata is structured rather than documentary information, and is thus more amenable to computation and automation. Conceptually, in terms of information content, a digital object should be considered as a composite entity composed of multiple data streams that can be labelled as data, metadata, documentation or paradata but all of which contribute to overall meaning and understanding. 

Organisations are likely to keep additional metadata or documentation information depending on curatorial capabilities or their internal process needs. Where such additional information exists online, it SHOULD be linked in the metadata for the objects to which it applies.
### Core Metadata
Cultural heritage materials are enormously diverse so the common attributes that can be used to construct generic interfaces for services such as discovery is somewhat limited. This specification is based on [Dublin Core](https://www.dublincore.org/specifications/) Elements with some additions from the more specific DC Terms. Standardised formats or controlled vocabularies SHOULD be used in preference to plaintext where this is indicated in parentheses. Note that some fields specifically refer to attributes of the physical object being digitised which are inherited by the digital object, while others are unique to the digital object.

This specification avoids making a distinction between the physical object and more abstract bibliographic entities such as [Works and Manifestations](https://www.ifla.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/assets/cataloguing/frbr/frbr.pdf) which apply to specific types of material. If required, the ability to link to more detailed metadata allows these types of relationships to be exposed.
#### Metadata about the Physical Object


| **DC**  | **Notes** |

| dc:titledc:descriptiondc:type ([DCMI Type Vocabulary](https://www.dublincore.org/specifications/dublin-core/dcmi-terms/#section-7))dc:related (URL)dc:creatordc:contributordcterms:created ([ISO8601](https://www.iso.org/standard/70908.html) including EDTF)dcterms:provenance (URL) | These MUST always be present*related* links to originators native metadata record(s) for physical object *created* is the creation date of the physical object*provenance* links to accession policy and/or accession details  |

### Mappings
The Dublin Core fields can be mapped to equivalent fields in other interoperability standards, such as the Europeana Data Model and LinkedArt. These are more expressive models which may permit a more nuanced expression of object metadata. Whichever standards is chosen, they MUST be serialised as [RDF/XML](https://www.w3.org/TR/rdf-syntax-grammar/) or JSON-LD for harvesting.  

| **Dublin Core** | **Europeana** **Data Model** **(edm:WebResource)** | **LinkedArt** **(abbreviated)** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| dc:title | dc:title | identified_by:      type: "Name" |
| dc:description | dc:description | referred_to_by:       type: "LinguisticObject",      classified_as:           type: "Type",          _label: "Description", |

### WikiData
Amongst other functions, [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Main_Page) provides useful resource for the identification and disambiguation of people and places. While it is not the authoritative source for information on these entities, it links to multiple sources which are. Therefore, for person and named place references, metadata SHOULD use links to WikiData references rather than specific sources, where they exist.    
### Multiple objects
Some objects might only be described at an aggregate level (e.g. boxes of material). This can be accommodated since there is not requirement that a record must link to a single IIIF object. There can be multiple *dc:references* links in a record.  
### Metadata-only objects
Some objects, for various reasons, may not be available online, but can still publish a useful metadata record that records the existence of the object and mechanisms for access. This can apply to both undigitised items and items that cannot be made available for legal or other reasons. Resources such [Early Modern Letters Online](https://emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/) demonstrate the significant research value of a suitably structured catalogue even in the absence of digitised surrogates.
### Notes
It is expected that organisations will be able to accommodate the required metadata within the systems and schemas that they already use. Formats are discussed for informational purposes but the emphasis is on ensuring the relevant data exists – mapping can be used to convert to suitable consumption forms when the need arises. However, the use of authorities and reference ontologies at source *is* strongly encouraged - these are discussed in more detail in the Access section.
## Imaging
This section will focus on minimum quality guidelines for 2D imaging materials. While it is possible to go into considerable detail on quality standards, many organisations will lack the technical capacity to conform to, or verify compliance, with such standards, rendering them moot. 
### Minimum Quality Standards
These are based on the National Archives’ “[Guidance on techniques for digitising documents and other materials](https://cdn.nationalarchives.gov.uk/documents/information-management/digitisation-at-the-national-archives.pdf)” which provide a good balance of detail vs practicality. 

- Full colour materials MUST be captured in 24-bit colour, and SHOULD use the [Enumerated sRGB](https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/6169) colourspace profile

- Microfilm and other monochrome material may OPTIONALLY be captured in  8-bit grayscale using the Enumerated greyscale colourspace profile

- Material between A5 and A3 in size MUST be captured at a minimum of 300 DPI, giving images between 4.5 and 17.5 megapixels

- Smaller objects MUST be imaged at an appropriately higher resolution to give a similar final image size, e.g.:

  - 6x4 inch photographs at a minimum of 600 DPI

  - 35mm transparencies at a minimum 4000 DPI

- For documents imaged on film, images SHOULD correspond to resolution equivalent to at least 300 DPI for the original document

- For larger objects, correspondingly, lower resolution imaging is permissible although high levels of detail in a large object may warrant higher resolution imaging.

- All images MUST have a sufficient clear border/margin to demonstrate to users that the entire item has been captured. Images MUST be captured against a neutral background that makes this easily discernable.  

- If a single image cannot capture an object in its entirety, there MUST be sufficient overlap between adjacent images (>10%) to allow images to be stitched together programatically.
### Recommended Reading
The National Archives’ Guidance document not only defines quality standards but provides useful guidance for a complete digitisation workflow, including handling guidance, metadata, and code recipes to create conformant [JPEG 2000](https://www.iso.org/standard/87632.html) files and validate them. 
## Preservation
The specification leverages existing digital preservation practice and certification rather than creating additional requirements. 

- Materials SHOULD be archived in a [CoreTrustSeal](https://www.coretrustseal.org/) certified repository or service.

- Digitised material SHOULD be archived in a format that is suitable for long-term preservation. For 2D imaged materials, [TIFF](https://www.iso.org/standard/34342.html) or uncompressed JPEG2000 are acceptable formats.   

- Metadata SHOULD be stored alongside image data in the native format used by the originating organisation. Archiving an additional version of the metadata formatted for compliance with N-RICH is OPTIONAL.  
## Access
### Document Format
N-RICH compliant documentation such as selection policies MUST use one of the following file formats:

- PDF/A: Specifically, PDF/A-1 ([ISO 19005-1](https://www.iso.org/standard/38920.html)) or PDF/A-2 ([ISO 19005-2](https://www.iso.org/standard/50655.html)) 

- [UTF-8 plaintext](https://www.w3schools.com/charsets/ref_html_utf8.asp)

- [Markdown](https://www.markdownguide.org/)

- [TeX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TeX)  
### Persistent Identifiers 
Objects (both physical and digital) and their metadata MUST be referenceable and accessible via persistent identifiers. [ARK](https://arks.org/) or [DataCite DOI](https://datacite.org/) SHOULD be used since they have provision for resolver services that can handle movement of objects between providers, enabling persistent references in the longer term.
### Image Access
Digitised images MUST be made available via an [International Image Interoperability Framework](https://iiif.io) service. IIIF also provides access to a rich set of presentation tools for pubic and scholarly access. IIIF services can operate over both JPEG2000 and TIFF images, so are compatible with preservation recommendations. 
### Metadata Access API
Metadata SHOULD be available for harvest via [OAI-PMH](https://www.openarchives.org/pmh/) which provides a mechanism for picking up just updated records, and collection-based filtering. Any additional metadata SHOULD also be made available in its native form via the same mechanism, signposted via *dc:*s*ource* or *dc:related* **links in the metadata. 
# Conclusions
This recommendation attempts to define a “minimum viable set” of standards and guidelines that balances useful interoperability, practical implementability for a wide range of organisation and extensibility to cover expansions in scope. To avoid reinventing the wheel, existing widely used approaches are chosen where possible. Many standards overlap, and where a choice has been made, it favours simplicity and flexibility for the pragmatic reason that such standards are easier to validate and map to other approaches. Nevertheless some gaps have been identified – which may be filled by further research or the development of new services. Of particular note are:

- Digitisation guidelines that cover the broader range of CH objects without being dependent on particular technical approaches

- Common authorities and ontologies that can form the basis for interoperability although preferential use of WikiData references mitigates this somewhat 

- Technical and staff capacity in many organisations to implement any recommendations

## Recommendations for N-RICH
As noted above, many smaller CH organisations lack the resources to maintain significant digital services in-house to support a digital research ecosystem. Therefore, there will be a need for N-RICH to provision a number of such central services, either operating them directly or brokering relationships with existing services. Examples include:

- Persistent Identifer minting (e.g. UK DataCite at the British Library) 

- Metadata/catalogue hosting and publication via OAI-PMH (e.g. Museum Data Service)

- IIIF hosting and publication

- Certified archival repository (e.g. existing Data Services)

Harvested metadata should be made available as Linked Data, leveraging the use of common authorities as outlined in the previous section. Linked data is also readily extensible, allowing more metadata to be aggregated and exposed as capabilities and practice improve. Frameworks such as [CIDOC-CRM](https://cidoc-crm.org/) provide a very generic approach that can be hard to use consistently whereas [Linked Art](https://linked.art/), while CIDOC compatible, provides a more prescriptive approach that is easier to use consistently and has mappings to other common CH standards such as SPECTRUM.
